name: Toothed gearing in the Hellenistic Greek world
summary: The surviving gears of the Antikythera Mechanism show that Hellenistic Greek craftsmen built trains of meshing bronze gear wheels.
description: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Greek geared device recovered from a Roman-era shipwreck off Antikythera, was dated by Freeth and colleagues to around the end of the second century BC and is the only dated evidence for Greek gear trains read for this record. Its gearing modelled lunar and solar cycles, and the 2006 Nature report calls it technically more complex than any known device for at least a millennium afterwards. Cicero's mention of a model of the heavens made by Archimedes suggests earlier devices of the kind, but no dated source for third-century gearing was read.

impact.note: Gear trains gave a new capability of passing and changing rotation (depth 2) and became a platform for mills, water-lifting, instruments, clocks and machinery over many generations (generativity 3); reach is held at 2, below the lead's 3, because the sources read do not trace the descent and China probably reached gearing separately.

date.label: around the end of the 2nd century BC
date.basis: Freeth and colleagues’ construction estimate. Jones finds the palaeographic evidence consistent with a wider range, extending up to the shipwreck.

events.statement: Freeth and colleagues estimate that the Greek geared device was made around the end of the second century BC. The date of construction remains uncertain. Its eclipse dial represented a 223-lunar-month cycle and marked possible solar or lunar eclipses. About one third of that scale survives. The upper back dial displayed a 19-year calendar of 235 lunar months in a five-turn spiral, consistent with the count in the back-cover inscription. Fragment B preserves part of the scale and part of the pointer, including the guiding pin that followed the gap between turns. Anastasiou and colleagues reconstruct the damaged mounting as a pointer that slid through its hub as the shaft turned. The final gear that drove the pointer is missing.

evidence.supports: constructed around the end of the second century bc
The spiral scale represents 223 lunar months, includes eclipse-possibility glyphs, and is about one third extant.

evidence.locator: §1, pp. 1–2, construction chronology; §2, pp. 3–4, Fig. 1 and Back Cover Inscription II.3
evidence.supports: The back-cover inscription gives 235 divisions. The surviving divisions accord with a five-turn spiral for the lunar months of the 19-year calendar. The construction estimate is uncertain within broader palaeographic and shipwreck limits.

evidence.locator: §1, PDF p. 1 and Fig. 1; §2.1, PDF pp. 3–5 and Figs. 3–5; §2.2, PDF pp. 5–7 and Fig. 6
evidence.supports: CT images show part of the Metonic spiral, pointer and damaged shaft mounting in Fragment B. The authors reconstruct a pin guided by the spiral slot and a pointer sliding through its rotating hub, using the inscription as a check. The last drive gear is missing.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Dated evidence for Greek gearing before the Antikythera Mechanism (Archimedes, Ktesibios, Philo of Byzantium, the Aristotelian Mechanical Problems) was not read; the lead's 3rd century BCE date is unsupported so far.
The earliest right-angle gearing in a working machine, such as a water-lifting wheel or mill, has no source yet.
Chinese Warring States and Han gearing, which the lead suspects is a separate origin, was not checked.
The place of manufacture is unknown; the Antikythera wreck is the findspot, not the place of making.

What securely dated, comparable inscriptions on bronze or independent archaeological evidence can narrow the construction date? Jones distinguishes the calendar’s epoch from the date the device was made.
The Babylonian-to-mechanism connection and any intervening transmission route need independent historical evidence; matching 223-month cycles alone do not establish a specific historical route.
Which surviving gear mounts and tooth counts constrain the missing end of the Metonic drive train? The recovered pointer and shaft constrain the display end of the drive.

research.note: The sources read date the Antikythera gearing but do not settle whether Greek gearing was independent of earlier gears elsewhere.

links.statement: Did the eclipse scheme represented on the Antikythera Mechanism draw on Babylonian astronomical methods involving the 223-month Saros?
links.scope: The eclipse dial only; a shared cycle does not itself establish how or from whom knowledge reached the makers.

evidence.supports: The dial represents a 223-month cycle with eclipse-possibility glyphs.
Late Babylonian astronomy used the 223-synodic-month Saros for eclipse possibilities.
